lessons.title: Parsing, FIRST/FOLLOW and LL/LR methods
lessons.intuition: A parser discovers grammatical structure in a token stream. Predictive parsing chooses productions before seeing their full result; bottom-up parsing recognizes handles after seeing the right-hand side. FIRST and FOLLOW sets summarize where grammar decisions can be made.

sections.title: FIRST and FOLLOW
sections.body: FIRST(α) contains terminals that can begin a string derived from α, plus ε if α can disappear. For a sequence, continue into later symbols when earlier ones are nullable. FOLLOW(A) contains terminals that can follow A in some sentential form; the start symbol includes end marker $. For A→αBβ, add FIRST(β) without ε to FOLLOW(B), and if β is nullable add FOLLOW(A).

sections.title: LL(1) prediction
sections.body: For A→α, put the production under terminals in FIRST(α); if α is nullable, also under FOLLOW(A). A conflict means the grammar is not LL(1) as written. Eliminate direct left recursion and factor common prefixes when appropriate, without assuming those changes fix every grammar. Recursive descent expands a leftmost derivation.

sections.title: Bottom-up parsing
sections.body: An LR parser tracks states representing viable prefixes, shifts input symbols and reduces a recognized right-hand side to its left-hand variable. Reductions reconstruct a rightmost derivation in reverse. Shift/reduce and reduce/reduce conflicts signal ambiguity or insufficient parsing information for the chosen method. LR handles a wider grammar class than LL(1).

sections.title: Deriving predictive choices and LR conflicts
sections.body: FIRST records terminals that can begin a derivation, whereas FOLLOW records terminals that can legally come immediately after a nonterminal in a sentential form. If a production’s right side can vanish, the parser must choose it when the lookahead belongs to the left side’s FOLLOW set. This is why nullable prefixes propagate FIRST from later symbols. Compute these sets repeatedly until no change; a single left-to-right sweep can miss indirect dependencies. LL(1) fails when two productions demand the same table cell. LR item sets instead encode how far productions have been recognized. An LR(0) completed item proposes a reduction independent of lookahead; SLR restricts reductions using FOLLOW; LR(1) items carry their own lookaheads. A shift/reduce or reduce/reduce conflict must be assessed for that specific table construction.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: If it vanishes, b is the first terminal of S. The terminal after nullable A therefore supplies another possible first symbol.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: \(FIRST(S)=\{a,b\}\); ε is absent because b cannot vanish. The entire right-hand side cannot vanish because b is mandatory, so epsilon must not enter FIRST(S).

examples.answer: \(FIRST(S)=\{a,b\}\); ε is absent because b cannot vanish.
examples.verification: S derives either ab or b under this grammar; their first terminals are exactly a and b.

lessons.title: Syntax-directed translation and runtime environments
lessons.intuition: A parse tree can carry semantic information such as expression values or types. Syntax-directed translation describes how this information moves. Runtime environments then arrange the storage needed when the translated program actually executes.

sections.title: Attributes and evaluation
sections.body: Synthesized attributes are computed from children and flow upward; inherited attributes receive information from a parent or relevant siblings. Semantic rules define dependencies, and a legal evaluation order respects that dependency graph. S-attributed definitions use only synthesized attributes and fit bottom-up evaluation naturally. L-attributed definitions restrict inherited dependencies for left-to-right evaluation.

sections.title: Translation actions
sections.body: An annotated syntax tree can compute expression types, values, offsets or emitted code. For E→E₁+T, a synthesized value rule may set E.val=E₁.val+T.val. Translation schemes embed actions in productions, so action placement determines execution order during a derivation. Parsing correctness alone does not guarantee the semantic actions are correct.

sections.title: Runtime storage
sections.body: An activation record can include arguments, return address, saved registers, locals and links. A dynamic link points to the caller’s frame; a static link supports lexical nesting and can point somewhere different. Stack allocation supports ordinary call-return lifetimes; heap allocation supports objects that outlive their creating call. Recursion needs separate frames even for the same function.

sections.title: Dependency graphs and environment links
sections.body: Attribute evaluation is a scheduling problem: each attribute value must be computed after the values it depends on. Synthesized attributes flow from child computations to a parent. Inherited attributes can flow from the parent or permitted siblings; not every inherited definition can be evaluated in a single left-to-right traversal. A cycle in the dependency graph prevents a simple evaluation order. At runtime, each call creates an activation record containing its own parameters, locals and return information under the calling convention. The dynamic link follows the chain of callers; the static link follows lexical nesting for nonlocal variable access. Recursive calls share the same source-level procedure but require distinct live records. Returning restores the caller’s execution context rather than reinitializing it.

The dynamic link references the caller’s activation and supports returning through the call chain. The static link references the lexically enclosing environment for access to nonlocal variables in nested procedures. Caller and lexical parent can differ, so those links are not interchangeable. A display is an alternative way to locate enclosing environments.
Storage allocation depends on lifetime: static-duration data can have a fixed location, stack allocation follows properly nested calls, and heap allocation supports lifetimes extending beyond a call. Returning releases the current frame and resumes the saved caller, not a fresh invocation. In GATE traces keep source-level names separate from their per-activation storage instances and identify whether nesting is lexical or merely a call relation.

example.prompt: Calls main→f→f occur recursively, and each f has local x.

steps.title: Create first frame
steps.explanation: The first f receives its own x object and return address to main.

steps.title: Recurse
steps.explanation: The second f gets a different x object and return address into the first f.

steps.title: Return
steps.explanation: Destroy the inner frame and resume the outer f with its saved x.

example.answer: The two f activations have distinct locals.

lessons.title: Intermediate code, local optimization and data-flow analysis
lessons.prerequisite: Expressions, CFG control flow and sets.
lessons.intuition: Intermediate representations expose simple operations and control flow so optimizations can reason about program behaviour. An optimization must preserve observable semantics; matching expression text is insufficient when operands may have changed.

sections.title: Three-address code and blocks
sections.body: Break compound expressions into assignments with at most a small fixed number of operands, such as t1=b*c; t2=a+t1. A basic block has one entry and no internal control-flow branch except at its end. Leaders include the first instruction, jump targets and instructions following jumps. A control-flow graph connects blocks by possible transfers.

sections.title: Local optimization
sections.body: Constant folding evaluates constant expressions; constant propagation substitutes known constants. Common-subexpression elimination reuses a previously computed expression only if its operands and relevant memory remain unchanged. Dead-code elimination removes computations whose results have no future use, provided they have no required side effects. Overflow, aliasing and floating-point rules can constrain algebraic transformations.

sections.title: Data flow
sections.body: Liveness is a backward may-analysis: OUT[B]=union of successors' IN sets; IN[B]=USE[B]∪(OUT[B]−DEF[B]). A variable is live if some continuation reads its current value before redefinition. Available expressions use forward propagation and typically intersection at joins because an expression must be available on every incoming path. Iterate finite-set equations to a fixed point.

sections.title: Why a fixed point represents all paths
sections.body: A variable is live at a program point if some path reads its present value before overwriting it. The word “some” makes the merge operator union: an obligation from any successor matters. At block exit, collect live-in sets of successors. Moving backward through the block, definitions kill the old value’s obligation and uses add obligations. Repeating across a loop is necessary because a successor may depend on information that returns through the back edge. In a finite powerset lattice with monotone transfers and the correct initialization, iteration stabilizes. Available expressions use an all-path requirement, so their meet is intersection instead. Common-subexpression elimination must establish operand stability on every relevant path; a potential aliasing write invalidates an otherwise visually repeated expression.

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: Emit t1=c*d because multiplication occurs first. The product is a prerequisite for addition, so its temporary must be defined first.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: Emit t2=b+t1. The addition refers to the already computed product temporary, preserving precedence without parentheses in the IR.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: Emit a=t2. The temporaries make dependencies explicit for later analysis. The final copy stores the expression result in a; temporary naming is arbitrary but dependency order is not.

examples.strategy: Emit one three-address operation per expression-tree computation in dependency order.
examples.answer: Emit a=t2. The temporaries make dependencies explicit for later analysis.
examples.verification: Substitute t1=c*d into t2=b+t1 and then into a=t2 to reconstruct a=b+c*d.

examples.prompt: Find live-in when USE={a}, DEF={b}, OUT={b,c}
steps: Remove definitions from OUT: {b,c}−{b}={c}.
Union with USE: {a}∪{c}={a,c}.
Thus b’s old value is not needed on entry, but a and c are.

pitfalls: Reusing a+b after assigning a is invalid without additional proof.
A may-analysis join uses union; must-properties often require intersection.
revision: Preserve side effects when removing dead results.

checks.prompt: Which join is used for live-variable OUT sets at multiple successors?
checks.hint: A variable is live if some future path needs it.
checks.explanation: Liveness is a may-property; union includes variables needed on any successor continuation.

checks.prompt: For t=4; u=t+6, what constant does propagation and folding assign to u?
checks.hint: Substitute t before arithmetic.

example.prompt: Translate a=b+c*d into three-address code.

example.prompt: One branch sets x=3, another x=3, then y=x+2. Change the second branch to x=4.
example.strategy: Equal branches → Fold → Different branches

steps.title: Equal branches
steps.explanation: With 3 on both paths, x is known as 3 at the merge.

steps.explanation: Propagation and folding are safe in that first program.

example.prompt: USE={a}, DEF={b}, OUT={b,c}. Find IN.

steps.title: Remove overwritten value
steps.explanation: Old b is not required just because new b is live later.

steps.title: Add direct use
steps.explanation: a’s incoming value is read within the block.

steps.title: Interpret
steps.explanation: The entering values of a and c are needed, while old b is not.

example.prompt: t1=a+b; c=7; t2=a+b; then change c=7 to a=7.

steps.title: Original operands
steps.explanation: Assigning c does not change a or b under the simple nonaliasing model.

name: Operating System
description: Processes, memory and the systems between them

lessons.title: System calls, processes, threads and IPC
lessons.intuition: A running program needs an execution context and protected resources. Processes give resource isolation; threads share much of that context while scheduling independently. Kernel entry is controlled because ordinary programs must not directly manipulate every device or other process.

sections.title: System calls and process states
sections.body: A system call enters privileged kernel handling through an architecture-defined trap mechanism. The kernel validates arguments and performs protected work. A process can be running, ready or blocked; blocked means waiting for an event, not merely waiting for CPU. A context switch saves and restores execution state and is distinct from any user-to-kernel mode transition.

sections.title: Threads and creation
sections.body: Threads in one process share an address space and open resources but normally have separate stacks and register contexts. A process creation mechanism such as fork copies a logical process context; modern implementations may initially share pages via copy-on-write. Different processes do not ordinarily share arbitrary writable memory unless explicitly arranged.

sections.title: IPC mechanisms
sections.body: Pipes and message queues move data with OS coordination. Shared memory lets processes access a common region and can reduce copying but requires synchronization. Signals provide notifications rather than general large-data transfer. Blocking calls suspend a caller until conditions are met; nonblocking calls return immediately with status. Choose the mechanism based on data size, synchronization and isolation needs.

sections.title: State changes and independent execution contexts
sections.body: A ready process can execute once given a processor; a blocked process cannot progress until its awaited event occurs. Preemption changes running to ready, while waiting for I/O changes running to blocked. I/O completion generally makes the process ready and does not guarantee immediate execution. Threads of one process commonly share address space, open resources and globals, but have their own registers and stacks. A switch must preserve enough execution context to resume the selected thread correctly. fork conceptually duplicates a process’s execution state and returns different values in parent and child; exec replaces the current program image without creating another process. A blocking system call can trigger a context switch, but a system call that completes immediately need not.

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: A process waiting for the scheduler after exhausting a time slice is ready. Its CPU work is executable but it has not been chosen; this is ready, not blocked.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: A process waiting for disk completion is blocked. The required data/event is not available, so assigning CPU alone cannot make the pending operation progress.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: When disk completion arrives, it usually becomes ready before the scheduler runs it again. Event completion removes the blocking condition; scheduling is a separate decision that selects among ready processes.

examples.strategy: Classify a process by what prevents its next instruction from executing.
examples.answer: When disk completion arrives, it usually becomes ready before the scheduler runs it again.
examples.verification: A ready process needs CPU selection; a blocked process needs an event first. These are different waiting queues.

examples.prompt: Two threads modify a shared global
steps: Both threads refer to the same process-global object.
Each still has its own local stack variables and instruction pointer.
Sharing the global creates a synchronization responsibility; having two stacks does not isolate global state.

pitfalls: A mode switch is not necessarily a process switch.
Shared memory does not automatically synchronize access.
revision: Process isolates resources; threads share address space.
Ready waits for CPU; blocked waits for an event.

checks.prompt: Four threads share one process. How many ordinary thread stacks are needed?
checks.hint: Each thread needs its own active call context.
checks.explanation: One stack per thread gives four stacks.

checks.prompt: A single CPU runs one thread at an instant in this simplified model. How many threads can be running simultaneously?
checks.hint: Ignore multicore hardware in the stated model.
checks.explanation: A single execution core runs one thread at a time.

A system call is a controlled request for an operating-system service such as reading a file, creating a process or mapping memory. A user program normally cannot execute privileged device or memory-management operations directly. A library wrapper prepares arguments and enters the kernel through an architecture-defined trap/syscall mechanism, after which the kernel validates the request and returns a result or error.
A mode switch changes privilege level; a context switch changes which execution context runs. They can occur together when a call blocks, but a quick service can return to the same thread without scheduling another. Not every library function invokes a system call: a string-length calculation may run entirely in user space.
Trace whether the service can complete immediately, whether it blocks awaiting an event and which resources it alters. The kernel must treat user pointers and lengths as untrusted inputs. Exec replaces the current program image without creating an additional process. Open-resource relationships and identifiers follow the specified OS semantics rather than a blanket “everything copied” rule.

Unconditional successful fork calls reached by every process double the population, but conditional calls, failures and exits alter that count. Waiting for a child and replacing an image are not additional process creations. In output traces, buffering and scheduling can matter beyond simply counting the number of executing print statements. Compare a process switch’s potentially different address space with a thread switch within one shared space, but avoid assuming zero cost for threads. A pipe supplies a byte stream with read/write endpoints; a message queue preserves its API’s message units; shared memory maps common storage into participating address spaces. Each mechanism has different copying, buffering and blocking behavior.
Shared memory removes the need to copy every communication item through a message channel, but needs synchronization to publish consistent state. A producer must not signal readiness before finishing the data write, and a consumer must not overwrite data before it is consumed. Pipes and sockets can return partial byte counts, so application framing remains necessary for multi-byte records.
Communication does not automatically imply mutual exclusion for every external resource. Analyze buffer capacity, endpoint closure and wait conditions. EOF on a pipe can depend on all writers being closed; an empty pipe with an open writer instead can block. example.prompt: One process executes two unconditional successful fork calls; no exits occur.

steps.explanation: Each of the two existing processes creates one child.

steps.title: Interpret
steps.explanation: There are four total processes, including the original, not four new children.

example.prompt: Two threads each have local y and both increment global x.
example.strategy: Local instances → Shared instance → Correctness

steps.title: Local instances
steps.explanation: Each thread has its own automatic y object.

steps.title: Shared instance
steps.explanation: Both name the same global x in the shared process space.

steps.title: Correctness
steps.explanation: Independent y updates need no mutual exclusion between these distinct objects; concurrent x updates can race.

example.verification: A process-global object does not become private simply because the modifying instructions run on different stacks.

tutorials.title: Pipes, messages and shared-memory IPC
tutorials.body:
Inter-process communication exchanges data or coordinates execution between processes. A pipe supplies a byte stream with read/write endpoints; a message queue preserves its API’s message units; shared memory maps common storage into participating address spaces. Each mechanism has different copying, buffering and blocking behavior.
Shared memory removes the need to copy every communication item through a message channel, but needs synchronization to publish consistent state. A producer must not signal readiness before finishing the data write, and a consumer must not overwrite data before it is consumed. Pipes and sockets can return partial byte counts, so application framing remains necessary for multi-byte records.
Communication does not automatically imply mutual exclusion for every external resource. Analyze buffer capacity, endpoint closure and wait conditions. EOF on a pipe can depend on all writers being closed; an empty pipe with an open writer instead can block. GATE deadlock examples may involve both parties waiting to receive before either sends, making protocol order as important as the chosen IPC facility.

example.prompt: A producer shares a buffer and a ready flag with a consumer.
example.strategy: Write payload → Publish safely → Consume

steps.title: Write payload
steps.explanation: The producer fills the buffer before publishing readiness.

steps.title: Publish safely
steps.explanation: Synchronization makes completed data visible and sets ready.

steps.title: Consume
steps.explanation: The consumer waits for readiness, reads the complete payload and acknowledges availability for reuse.

example.answer: A synchronized publish/consume protocol is needed.
example.verification: A shared address alone does not guarantee that the consumer sees a complete, current message.

lessons.title: Concurrency, mutexes and semaphores
lessons.intuition: Concurrency allows operations to overlap in time even on one CPU. If a shared update consists of separate read and write steps, scheduling can interleave those steps and lose information. Correct synchronization constrains interleavings, not just the final line of source code.

sections.title: Race conditions and critical sections
sections.body: A data race involves unsynchronized conflicting accesses under the applicable memory model; broader race conditions make correctness depend on timing. A critical section protects shared invariants. Mutual exclusion ensures at most one entrant, while progress and bounded waiting address liveness. Declaring an object volatile is not a substitute for atomicity or a lock.

sections.title: Mutex and semaphore
sections.body: A mutex gives exclusive ownership around a protected region. A semaphore maintains a count with atomic wait and signal operations. wait decrements when available or blocks; signal returns a permit or wakes a waiter under the implementation model. A binary semaphore can coordinate single access but ownership semantics need not match a mutex. Counting semaphores manage multiple identical resources.

sections.title: Producer–consumer
sections.body: For a capacity-N buffer, use empty=N, full=0 and a mutex for buffer manipulation. Producer waits for empty then locks, inserts, unlocks and signals full; consumer symmetrically waits for full and later signals empty. Waiting for availability while holding the buffer mutex can block the other side from making progress.

sections.title: Proving safety separately from progress
sections.body: An invariant such as “at most one thread is in the critical section” is a safety property: no bad simultaneous access occurs. Progress asks that eligible attempts can eventually enter; bounded waiting strengthens this with a bound on overtaking. A design can be safe and still starve a thread forever. Locking only the write in a read-modify-write operation is insufficient because another thread may change the value after an unprotected read. Protect the whole invariant-preserving update. Condition variables normally wait by atomically releasing the associated lock and sleeping, then reacquire the lock before returning. Recheck the predicate in a loop because wakeups and competing consumers may leave it false. Semaphores store permits, whereas a condition notification does not generally store a future entitlement.

examples.prompt: Show a lost update for shared x=0

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: Thread A reads 0; thread B reads 0. Both reads can occur before either write because the compound update is not protected atomically.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: A computes and stores 1; B also computes and stores 1. Each computation uses its own saved read value zero, so both stores write the same one.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: Two increments finish with x=1 rather than 2. Locking the whole read-modify-write operation prevents that interleaving. The final store overwrites the same value instead of accumulating both increments. The protected region must include the read.

examples.strategy: Split increment into read, compute and store, then interleave legal events.
examples.answer: Two increments finish with x=1 rather than 2. Locking the whole read-modify-write operation prevents that interleaving.
examples.verification: The interleaving respects each thread’s local order yet ends at 1. Serializing complete increments gives 2, proving the race changes the outcome.

steps: Initialize semaphore count to 3.
Three successful waits consume all permits, leaving 0.
A fourth requester must block until some owner signals, restoring a permit.

Incorrect lock order can introduce deadlock.

Counting semaphore permits model resource capacity.

steps.title: First waits
steps.explanation: Three successful waits consume all permits and occupy the devices.

steps.title: Fourth wait
steps.explanation: No permit remains, so the fourth client blocks.

steps.title: Release
steps.explanation: A holder signals after releasing its device, allowing one waiting client to proceed.

lessons.title: Deadlock, avoidance and safe states
lessons.intuition: Deadlock is a circular dependency in which participants cannot proceed. A state can be unsafe without already being deadlocked: unsafe means future declared resource demands might prevent a guaranteed completion order.

sections.title: Necessary conditions
sections.body: The standard Coffman conditions are mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no forced resource preemption and circular wait. All are necessary in the usual resource-allocation model. Prevention deliberately breaks one, for example imposing a global resource-acquisition order to rule out circular waiting.

sections.title: Avoidance with Banker
sections.body: Each process declares its maximum demand. Need=Max−Allocation, and Available is the currently free vector. A safety test repeatedly finds a process with Need≤Work, assumes it completes, and adds its Allocation back to Work. If all can be removed, the resulting sequence certifies safety. A resource request is tentatively granted only if the new state passes the test.

sections.title: Detection and model limits
sections.body: In a single-instance resource graph, a cycle corresponds to deadlock; with multiple instances, a cycle need not be sufficient. Detection examines actual allocations and outstanding requests rather than maximum future claims. Recovery can terminate or roll back processes or preempt suitable resources. Starvation is indefinite denial to a participant while others may still progress, which differs from deadlock.

sections.title: What a safety certificate guarantees
sections.body: A safe state admits an order in which every process can receive its full remaining declared claim, complete and release resources. The safety algorithm does not predict actual scheduling; it constructs a witness that the system could satisfy even worst-case claims. Work is a temporary available-resource vector and must be compared componentwise with Need. Finishing a hypothetical process adds its held allocation to Work, producing a monotone increase. If no unfinished process is feasible, the current state lacks a safety certificate under those maximum claims. That is an unsafe-state finding, not proof that every process is already blocked. Deadlock prevention removes a necessary condition such as circular wait; avoidance uses future-claim information; detection evaluates actual outstanding requests and allocations.

examples.prompt: Check safety: Available=1, P1 allocation=1/max=2, P2 allocation=1/max=3

steps.title: Compute remaining needs
steps.explanation: Maximum claims are totals, not additional requests. Need is the remaining claim after currently held resources.

steps.title: Finish P1 hypothetically
steps.explanation: P1 can receive its remaining resource and complete. In the safety algorithm, adding its original allocation captures the net increase after borrowed Work is returned.

steps.title: Finish P2 hypothetically
steps.explanation: Every process can finish in order P1,P2, so this is a safe sequence. P2 could not have been chosen first at Work=1.

examples.given: One resource type. Available=1; P1 holds 1 with maximum 2; P2 holds 1 with maximum 3.
examples.goal: Determine whether the state is safe.
examples.strategy: Use a private Work variable and find an order of hypothetical completions.
examples.answer: Safe; a safety witness is P1 followed by P2.
examples.verification: Final Work=3 equals total system resources: initial Available 1 plus both original allocations. Adding Max instead would incorrectly create resources.

steps: Every thread must acquire lock A before lock B.
A thread holding B cannot wait for A because that acquisition order is disallowed.
This removes a possible A↔B circular wait, though other correctness concerns still need analysis.

pitfalls: Unsafe is not synonymous with already deadlocked.
A cycle is not sufficient in every multiple-instance resource graph.
revision: Safety test simulates finishing processes and releasing allocations.

checks.explanation: Unsafe means no safe sequence under declared maximum demands. Current requests may still permit progress, so actual deadlock is not established.
options: It lacks a guaranteed safe completion sequence but may not be deadlocked yet
It always has zero available resources

lessons.title: CPU and I/O scheduling
lessons.intuition: Scheduling chooses which waiting work receives a resource next. A schedule should be traced on a time axis using arrival times and preemption rules. Waiting, response and turnaround times describe different experiences and should not be interchanged.

sections.title: CPU metrics
sections.body: Turnaround=completion−arrival. In the single CPU-burst model, waiting=turnaround−burst. Response time measures first execution−arrival. FCFS serves arrival order and may create a convoy behind a long job. Nonpreemptive SJF picks the shortest available next burst; shortest-remaining-time-first is its preemptive variant. Future arrivals cannot be scheduled before they exist.

sections.title: Round-robin
sections.body: Run each ready process for at most quantum q, then requeue if unfinished. Small q improves opportunities for responsiveness but raises context-switch overhead; very large q approaches FCFS. At simultaneous arrivals/completions define the queue tie convention. Priority scheduling may starve low-priority work; aging can increase priority over time.

sections.title: Disk scheduling
sections.body: FCFS follows request order. SSTF picks the nearest requested cylinder, potentially starving distant requests. SCAN moves in a direction and reverses, while LOOK reverses at the last request rather than physical end. C-SCAN serves one direction with a return movement. Total head travel depends on the initial position, direction and whether endpoint movement counts.

sections.title: Use events rather than averaging burst lengths
sections.body: A scheduling decision can occur at an arrival, completion, quantum expiration or blocking event, depending on the policy. In nonpreemptive SJF, a newly arriving shorter job does not displace the running job; SRTF compares remaining time at relevant arrivals. Round robin appends unfinished work to a ready queue at quantum expiry, but arrivals and a simultaneous expiry need an explicitly stated tie convention. Waiting time is accumulated time in the ready queue. For a single CPU-only burst, turnaround equals waiting plus service, which permits subtraction; for workloads with I/O, blocked time must also be accounted for. Response time ends at the first CPU dispatch. Draw a separate timeline for each policy, and calculate per-process values before taking their arithmetic mean.

examples.prompt: FCFS with both arrivals at 0 and bursts 3,5

steps.title: Build the Gantt chart
steps.explanation: Both are present initially. The stated order breaks the arrival tie; a different tie order would change mean waiting.

steps.title: Calculate waiting
steps.explanation: FCFS is nonpreemptive here, so each process waits only before its first execution.

steps.title: Calculate turnaround
steps.explanation: Turnaround includes both waiting and CPU service. It is measured from arrival to completion.

examples.given: P1 and P2 arrive at time 0; CPU bursts 3 and 5; FCFS order P1,P2; no switch overhead.
examples.goal: Compute mean waiting and turnaround times.
examples.strategy: Construct the timeline, then calculate each metric separately.
examples.answer: Mean waiting 1.5; mean turnaround 5.5 time units.
examples.verification: For each process T=W+B: 3=0+3 and 8=3+5. Mean burst 4 plus mean waiting 1.5 equals mean turnaround 5.5.

steps: Closest is 55, movement 5.
From 55, closest remaining is 80, movement 25.
Finish at 10, movement 70. Total movement=5+25+70=100 cylinders.

Disk LOOK and SCAN endpoint rules differ.

lessons.concept: Scheduling chooses which waiting work receives a resource next. A schedule should be traced on a time axis using arrival times and preemption rules. Waiting, response and turnaround times describe different experiences and should not be interchanged.
lessons.method:
CPU scheduling chooses among ready processes. FCFS uses arrival order without ordinary burst preemption. Nonpreemptive SJF chooses the shortest available burst when dispatching; SRTF instead can preempt for a smaller remaining time. Neither can choose a job that has not yet arrived. Round robin assigns a time quantum and returns unfinished work to the ready queue.
Build a Gantt chart at arrivals, completions and quantum expirations. Turnaround is completion minus arrival; response is first dispatch minus arrival. For CPU-only single-burst workloads, waiting equals turnaround minus service. With I/O, blocked time needs separate accounting. Tie order and simultaneous arrivals/quantum events can change exact answers.
A small quantum improves responsiveness at the expense of frequent switch overhead; a very large one approaches FCFS. SJF’s mean-wait properties assume known burst information and specified workloads, not arbitrary future knowledge. Compute metrics per process before averaging; an average CPU burst alone does not determine an average waiting time. Include switch costs only if the question supplies them. For a moving-head disk model, service order determines head movement. FCFS serves requests in arrival order; SSTF chooses the nearest pending track and can starve distant requests. SCAN moves in one direction serving encountered requests, reaches the specified boundary and reverses. LOOK reverses at the last pending request instead of necessarily visiting the physical end.
C-SCAN services in one direction and wraps; C-LOOK wraps between extreme pending requests. Whether wrap or boundary motion is counted must follow the question. Direction is part of initial state, not something chosen retrospectively to improve a result. Real solid-state storage does not incur this same seek-distance model.
Sum absolute differences between consecutive visited positions, including required boundary and wrap legs. Do not replace movement by final-minus-initial displacement, which cancels reversed motion. If new requests arrive dynamically, scheduling can differ from a static queue calculation. GATE problems often distinguish SCAN from LOOK through the otherwise easy-to-forget boundary trip. Turnaround=completion−arrival. In the single CPU-burst model, waiting=turnaround−burst. Response time measures first execution−arrival. FCFS serves arrival order and may create a convoy behind a long job. Nonpreemptive SJF picks the shortest available next burst; shortest-remaining-time-first is its preemptive variant. Future arrivals cannot be scheduled before they exist. Run each ready process for at most quantum q, then requeue if unfinished. Small q improves opportunities for responsiveness but raises context-switch overhead; very large q approaches FCFS. At simultaneous arrivals/completions define the queue tie convention. Priority scheduling may starve low-priority work; aging can increase priority over time. FCFS follows request order. SSTF picks the nearest requested cylinder, potentially starving distant requests. SCAN moves in a direction and reverses, while LOOK reverses at the last request rather than physical end. C-SCAN serves one direction with a return movement. Total head travel depends on the initial position, direction and whether endpoint movement counts. A scheduling decision can occur at an arrival, completion, quantum expiration or blocking event, depending on the policy. In nonpreemptive SJF, a newly arriving shorter job does not displace the running job; SRTF compares remaining time at relevant arrivals. Round robin appends unfinished work to a ready queue at quantum expiry, but arrivals and a simultaneous expiry need an explicitly stated tie convention. Waiting time is accumulated time in the ready queue. For a single CPU-only burst, turnaround equals waiting plus service, which permits subtraction; for workloads with I/O, blocked time must also be accounted for. Response time ends at the first CPU dispatch. Draw a separate timeline for each policy, and calculate per-process values before taking their arithmetic mean.

lessons.title: Memory management, virtual memory and file systems
lessons.intuition: Virtual memory separates a program’s address space from physical placement. A translation may be missing from the TLB even when the page is resident; a page fault instead means the required resident mapping cannot complete normally and OS handling is needed.

sections.title: Paging and translation
sections.body: Split a virtual address into page number and offset. The page table maps the page number to a physical frame; offset is unchanged. A TLB caches translations, not ordinarily the data itself. Page-table size depends on page count and entry size. Larger pages reduce entry count but can increase internal fragmentation. Segmentation models variable-size logical regions and has different allocation trade-offs.

sections.title: Replacement and faults
sections.body: Demand paging loads pages when first needed or after eviction. FIFO removes the oldest loaded page, LRU the least recently used, and optimal the page whose next use is farthest in the future. Optimal needs future knowledge and is a benchmark. FIFO can exhibit Belady’s anomaly; LRU is a stack algorithm and does not. Too few frames for active working sets can cause thrashing.

sections.title: File organization
sections.body: Directories map names to metadata or file identifiers. Contiguous allocation supports simple sequential/random positioning but complicates growth; linked allocation traverses pointers; indexed allocation stores block pointers in an index structure. Free-space maps, access permissions and crash consistency are separate responsibilities. An inode-like record can point to direct and indirect block addresses.

sections.title: Page-table walks and replacement state
sections.body: Paging preserves the offset because a page and its physical frame have equal size. The page-table entry supplies the frame number and permission/residency metadata. A TLB caches recent translations, so a miss can be resolved by an ordinary page-table walk without disk access. A nonresident page is a page fault and invokes a much slower path that can include eviction, dirty-page writeback, load and restart. Replacement policies have distinct state: FIFO records load order, LRU records last reference, and optimal replacement uses the future reference sequence as a comparison benchmark. A hit changes LRU recency but not FIFO age. Compare page faults on the same initial frame state and reference string. Effective access time needs complete mutually exclusive paths; a miss penalty defined as extra time must not have the baseline counted twice.

lessons.title: File systems, allocation and free-space management
lessons.intuition: A file system connects human names and byte offsets to physical blocks. File metadata, block allocation and directory structure have different responsibilities. A lookup cost depends on which metadata is cached and which indirection levels must be read.

sections.title: Allocation choices
sections.body: Contiguous allocation stores consecutive blocks and computes block location by start+index, but growth and external fragmentation are challenges. Linked allocation stores the next block address in each block or a separate table; random access requires following links unless indexed metadata helps. Indexed allocation keeps a pointer array or tree so a chosen logical block can be located without reading all previous data blocks.

sections.title: Direct and indirect pointers
sections.body: An inode-style record can have several direct pointers, a pointer to one indirect block of addresses, and further levels. If a block has B bytes and an address occupies a bytes, an indirect block holds B/a pointers ignoring metadata. A double-indirect path can cover (B/a)² data blocks. Access cost includes metadata blocks that are not already cached.

sections.title: Directories and consistency
sections.body: Directory entries connect names to file identifiers; hard links can give multiple names for the same file object while symbolic links contain a path to be resolved. Free-space bitmaps or lists track available blocks. Updates spanning allocation, data and metadata need crash consistency, often via journaling or copy-on-write techniques. File permissions control access independently of block placement.

sections.title: Data reachability, metadata and disk movement
sections.body: An indirect block contains addresses, not user payload. If a block contains p addresses, one single-indirect pointer reaches p data blocks, a double-indirect pointer reaches up to p², and a triple-indirect pointer up to p³. Add direct blocks, then multiply reachable data blocks by data-block size. Metadata space and metadata I/O are separate counts: following a double-indirect pointer may read two index blocks before the data block unless cached. Linked allocation makes sequential access natural but locating an arbitrary logical block requires link traversal. Contiguous allocation permits arithmetic location but constrains growth and can suffer external fragmentation. Disk scheduling calculations apply to a moving-head model: add absolute differences of consecutive head positions and follow the specified direction/end/wrap rules.

tutorials.title: Inodes and direct/indirect capacity
tutorials.body:
An inode-style file record stores metadata and addresses for data, often mixing direct pointers with single-, double- and triple-indirect pointers. A direct pointer names one data block. A single-indirect pointer names an index block of data-block addresses; double indirection adds another index level. The directory maps a filename to a file identifier/inode, rather than necessarily storing all payload addresses itself.
With B-byte index blocks and p-byte pointers, up to floor(B/p) addresses fit after accounting for reserved metadata. Capacity for d direct plus one pointer at each of three indirect levels is B(d+k+k²+k³) data bytes under the ideal layout. Index blocks consume additional physical storage and I/O but are not user-data blocks.
Random-read cost depends on how many metadata pages are already cached and which pointer level contains the requested logical block. An inode can exist with several hard-link names; filename count need not equal object count. Follow exact pointer counts and block sizes in GATE problems instead of assuming the familiar Unix layout is universal.

example.prompt: Ten direct pointers and one single-indirect pointer; block 1024 bytes, pointer 4 bytes.
example.strategy: Index capacity → Reachable data blocks → Payload capacity

steps.title: Index capacity
steps.explanation: The indirect block stores 256 addresses.

steps.title: Reachable data blocks
steps.explanation: Direct and indirect targets add.

steps.title: Payload capacity
steps.explanation: Exclude the index block’s own metadata bytes.

example.answer: Maximum data capacity 272,384 bytes under this layout.
example.verification: The single-indirect block adds one metadata block to allocated storage, not another 1024 bytes of file data.

name: Databases
description: Model, query and protect your data

lessons.title: ER modelling, relational schemas and integrity
lessons.intuition: A database model captures which facts exist and how they relate. ER diagrams express entities and relationships at a conceptual level; relational schemas encode them as tables with keys and constraints that prevent invalid states.

sections.title: ER concepts and mapping
sections.body: Entities have identifying attributes; relationships link entities with cardinality and participation constraints. A one-to-many relationship is often represented by a foreign key on the many side. A many-to-many relationship becomes its own relation with foreign keys to both sides and any relationship attributes. Weak entities require an owner key plus their partial identifier.

sections.title: Relational keys
sections.body: A superkey uniquely determines a tuple; a candidate key is a minimal superkey. Choose one candidate as primary key. Keys can span multiple attributes, and additional unique constraints can express alternate keys. Relations in the mathematical model are sets of tuples, unlike SQL’s default duplicate-preserving query results.

sections.title: Integrity
sections.body: Domain constraints restrict value types/ranges; entity integrity requires primary-key values not be NULL; referential integrity requires a non-NULL foreign key to match an allowed referenced key. Deleting a referenced tuple may be rejected or trigger defined cascading/set-null actions. A foreign key need not be unique on the referencing side.

sections.title: Keys express constraints rather than sample coincidences
sections.body: A candidate key is a minimal set of attributes that uniquely identifies every possible legal row under the schema constraints. Seeing distinct names in one sample table does not prove name is a key. A superkey may contain unnecessary attributes; a primary key is one chosen candidate key. A relationship can need its own attributes: a grade belongs to a student’s enrollment in a course, rather than to the student or course alone. For repeated enrollments, the student/course pair ceases to identify each event and a term or attempt identifier is needed. Weak entities depend on an owner plus their partial key. Foreign-key constraints enforce that referenced rows exist, but cardinality, nullability and total participation can need additional uniqueness or application/database constraints.

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: Student has key student_id; Course has key course_id. Entity identifiers are inherited into the relationship to state which student and which course participate.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: Because many students take many courses, create Enrollment(student_id,course_id,grade). Neither a student nor a course alone identifies an enrollment, because each can participate many times.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: The pair can be its key if each student takes each course once, and both identifiers are foreign keys. Repeated offerings would need an additional term/attempt attribute. The pair is minimal only under the one-enrollment-per-student/course assumption; adding repeated terms changes that constraint.

examples.answer: The pair can be its key if each student takes each course once, and both identifiers are foreign keys. Repeated offerings would need an additional term/attempt attribute.
examples.verification: One student in two courses and two students in one course produce distinct pairs without duplicating entity details or losing relationship grades.

example.prompt: Student_id uniquely identifies students. Classify {student_id} and {student_id,name}.

steps.title: Minimality

lessons.title: Relational algebra, tuple calculus and SQL
lessons.intuition: A query describes a derived relation. Algebra describes operations to produce it, while calculus describes a logical condition on desired tuples. SQL uses related ideas but adds practical semantics for duplicates, NULL and grouping.

sections.title: Algebra and calculus
sections.body: Selection σ filters tuples; projection π keeps named columns and removes duplicates in set-based algebra. Cartesian product pairs every tuple; a join filters combinations by a condition. Union and difference require compatible schemas. Tuple relational calculus uses predicates on tuples; safe/range-restricted expressions ensure finite, domain-independent results.

sections.title: SQL order and joins
sections.body: Conceptually FROM/JOIN establishes sources, WHERE filters rows, GROUP BY forms groups, HAVING filters groups, SELECT chooses expressions, and ORDER BY orders results. An inner join requires a match; an outer join also retains unmatched rows with NULL-filled columns. Filtering an outer-joined table in WHERE can discard the unmatched rows and change the intended semantics.

sections.title: Duplicates, aggregates and NULL
sections.body: SELECT ordinarily keeps duplicates; DISTINCT removes them. COUNT(*) counts rows, while COUNT(column) counts non-NULL values. SUM/AVG ordinarily ignore NULL inputs. Comparisons involving NULL usually yield UNKNOWN; WHERE retains only TRUE. Use IS NULL rather than =NULL. SQL OR/AND follows three-valued logic in such cases.

sections.title: Trace bags, nulls and grouping explicitly
sections.body: Under SQL bag semantics, a join can multiply duplicates: if a key has two matching left rows and three matching right rows, their equality join contributes six rows. DISTINCT removes duplicates at its specified stage and cannot be assumed throughout. WHERE evaluates predicates on source rows, then GROUP BY partitions survivors and HAVING filters completed groups. Null comparisons normally yield UNKNOWN, so NULL=NULL does not become TRUE; use IS NULL to test nullness. COUNT(*) counts rows, while COUNT(column) and AVG(column) ignore nulls. For an empty input without grouping, COUNT returns zero while many other aggregates return NULL. NOT IN can be poisoned by a null comparison; reasoning through the three-valued truth conditions is safer than blindly rewriting it as an anti-join.

examples.prompt: Count students per department with at least three students

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: Group Student rows by dept. Rows with the same department value contribute to the same aggregate group.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: Use SELECT dept, COUNT(*) FROM Student GROUP BY dept HAVING COUNT(*)>=3. COUNT(*) counts the rows in each group and HAVING applies the threshold to that computed group result.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: The group filter belongs in HAVING; WHERE cannot directly filter by the completed aggregate count. A row-level WHERE condition cannot use the aggregate count of a group that has not yet been formed.

examples.strategy: Form groups before evaluating a predicate over their aggregate count.
examples.answer: The group filter belongs in HAVING; WHERE cannot directly filter by the completed aggregate count.
examples.verification: A department with two rows is absent, one with three rows appears with count 3; SELECT and GROUP BY use the same grouping attribute.

Relational algebra builds relations through operations. Selection σ filters tuples by a predicate and preserves attributes. Projection π keeps specified attributes and removes duplicate resulting tuples under set semantics. Cartesian product forms every tuple pairing; a theta join filters that product by a condition. Natural join matches all shared attribute names and includes one copy of each shared attribute.
Union, intersection and difference require compatible schemas/domains. Rename resolves attribute ambiguity and enables a relation to join with itself. Division expresses an “associated with every required value” query by finding candidate values with no missing required partner.
Operator order matters: projecting away an attribute before a selection that needs it makes that predicate unavailable. A natural join can accidentally match an unrelated shared name, so use explicit conditions when names do not encode the intended relationship. SQL may retain duplicates, giving different cardinalities from set algebra. GATE query-equivalence problems require the stated semantics and constraints, not just similar-looking expressions. Free tuple variables describe the output; bound variables express existence or universal requirements. This connects database querying to first-order logic.

An unconstrained negation such as all tuples not in a finite relation can range over infinitely many possibilities and is unsafe. Negation becomes meaningful when candidates are bounded by a relation.
Existential predicates express matching joins; universal requirements can be rewritten as absence of a counterexample. Quantifier scope matters just as in logic: one common witness differs from a witness per candidate. For GATE, identify output variables, candidate domain and predicate meaning before translating to algebra or SQL. lessons.title: Functional dependencies and normal forms
lessons.intuition: Normalization controls redundancy caused by dependencies. A dependency is a rule about every valid database state, not a coincidence in one sample table. Begin by computing keys; normal-form tests depend on superkeys and prime attributes.

sections.title: Closure and inference
sections.body: \(X\to Y\) says equal values on X force equal values on Y. Attribute closure X⁺ starts with X and repeatedly adds RHS attributes whose LHS is already present. If X⁺ contains the whole schema, X is a superkey; remove redundant attributes to test minimality. Armstrong’s reflexivity, augmentation and transitivity support sound dependency inference.

sections.title: 2NF, 3NF and BCNF
sections.body: After atomic-value 1NF, 2NF rules out dependence of a nonprime attribute on a proper subset of a candidate key. In 3NF, every nontrivial X→A has X a superkey or A prime, meaning in some candidate key. BCNF drops the prime-attribute exception and requires every nontrivial determinant to be a superkey. BCNF implies 3NF, but not conversely.

sections.title: Decomposition
sections.body: Lossless join means decomposed relations reconstruct exactly the original valid relation, with no spurious tuples. For a binary decomposition into R1,R2, their intersection determining all of R1 or all of R2 under F⁺ is the usual lossless criterion. Dependency preservation permits checking original dependencies without joining. These are separate properties; a BCNF decomposition can lose dependency preservation.

sections.title: Closure, decomposition and independent guarantees
sections.body: Attribute closure is an inference procedure: start with X, apply any FD whose entire left side is present, add its right side, and repeat to a fixed point. A key needs closure equal to all relation attributes and minimality under attribute removal. BCNF restricts every nontrivial determinant to a superkey; 3NF additionally permits a prime right-hand attribute. Lossless decomposition means every legal original relation is exactly reconstructed by joining its projections. It does not merely mean that tables share a column. lessons.title: File organization and B/B+ tree indexing
lessons.intuition: An index is an auxiliary route to data, not the data model itself. On-disk indexes use high branching factors to reduce expensive page reads. Equality and range queries can prefer different organizations.

sections.title: File layout
sections.body: Heap files place records in convenient free space and favour insertion without key order. Sorted files favour ordered scans but make insertion maintenance costly. Hash organization targets equality buckets and generally does not preserve ordering. A clustered organization aligns data placement with index order; a secondary index may require scattered data-page fetches.

sections.title: B-tree family
sections.body: B and B+ trees remain balanced and store many separator keys per page. In a common B+ design, internal nodes guide search while data entries are at leaves, which are linked for range scans. Definitions of “order” vary: read whether it means maximum children, maximum keys or minimum occupancy. Splits, redistribution and merges preserve occupancy and balance.

sections.title: Cost reasoning
sections.body: With fanout f and many entries, height grows roughly logarithmically in f. Point search follows one root-to-leaf path; a range search locates its starting leaf then walks linked leaves. Dense indexes have an entry for every relevant key/record convention; sparse indexes have selected entries and ordinarily require ordered data. Include data-page reads separately when an index does not contain the required record.

sections.title: Derive capacity from page layout
sections.body: An internal B+ tree page with f children normally needs f pointers and f−1 separator keys; a leaf page instead needs key/record entries and a next-leaf pointer, potentially with other metadata. Subtract reserved bytes before deriving each capacity. Maximum fanout is not minimum occupancy: split rules and root exceptions affect minimum and maximum tree heights. Search chooses an internal pointer using separators until a leaf, then checks the actual key. A range query locates its first leaf once and follows leaf links, but fetching records through an unclustered index can add scattered data-page I/O. A clustered layout tends to group nearby key values in nearby data pages. Counting tree levels alone estimates index traversal, not necessarily the entire query’s disk cost.

examples.prompt: Estimate maximum leaves for a B+ tree with 3 levels and fanout 4

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: The root is level 1 and can point to 4 internal nodes. Level numbering starts at the root as level 1; three levels therefore contain two pointer expansions.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: Each internal node can point to 4 leaves. Each of the four internal nodes can supply four independent leaf children under the maximum-fanout assumption.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: Maximum leaves=4×4=16, excluding leaf entry capacity from this count. This is the maximum number of leaf pages, not the maximum records. Record capacity additionally requires entries per leaf.

examples.strategy: Count child pointers per level and keep leaf entry capacity out of leaf-node count.
examples.answer: Maximum leaves=4×4=16, excluding leaf entry capacity from this count.
examples.verification: Level counts are 1,4,16. Multiplying by four a third time would erroneously count an extra level.

lessons.title: Transactions, serializability and concurrency control
lessons.intuition: Transactions group operations into a unit whose intermediate effects must be controlled. Concurrency can improve throughput, but interleavings must preserve an allowed relationship to serial execution and support recovery when work fails.

sections.title: ACID and anomalies
sections.body: Atomicity gives all-or-nothing effects; consistency preserves declared invariants when transactions themselves are correct; isolation controls interference; durability preserves committed effects after recovery. Lost updates overwrite another transaction’s changes. Dirty reads observe uncommitted writes. Nonrepeatable reads and phantoms involve changing rows or predicate result sets across reads.

sections.title: Conflict serializability
sections.body: Two operations conflict if they are in different transactions, access the same item, and at least one writes. Add Ti→Tj when Ti’s conflicting operation precedes Tj’s. The schedule is conflict serializable iff this precedence graph is acyclic; a topological order gives an equivalent serial ordering. Read-read pairs create no edge. Conflict serializability is stronger than some other semantic notions of serializability.

sections.title: Locks and recovery
sections.body: Two-phase locking first acquires locks, then releases without acquiring new ones. It guarantees conflict serializability under the standard model but can deadlock. Strict variants retain required exclusive locks until commit/abort to prevent cascading effects. Write-ahead logging requires appropriate log records be durable before related dirty data pages are written. Recovery may redo committed work and undo uncommitted work according to its logging scheme.

sections.title: Three graphs of reasoning: conflict, reads and locks
sections.body: Conflict ordering constrains transactions when actions from different transactions touch the same item and at least one is a write. Read/read order adds no conflict edge. A directed cycle prevents any serial order satisfying all conflict constraints. Recovery instead follows which write supplied each read: committing a reader before that writer risks a committed dependency on an aborted value. Cascadeless schedules prevent reading uncommitted writes; strict schedules also prevent overwriting uncommitted writes. Two-phase locking forbids new lock acquisitions after the first release and guarantees conflict serializability, but can deadlock. Strict 2PL holds exclusive locks until completion, preventing dirty reads/writes of protected items; terminology for holding all locks is often called rigorous 2PL. Distinguish protocol rules from properties inferred for one particular schedule.

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: W1(X) before R2(X) adds \(T_1\to T_2\). A write followed by another transaction’s read conflicts, so any equivalent serial order must place T1 before T2.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: W2(Y) before R1(Y) adds \(T_2\to T_1\). The conflict on Y imposes the opposite ordering, T2 before T1.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: The graph has a cycle, so the schedule is not conflict serializable. No serial transaction order can satisfy both directions; the two-edge cycle is a certificate of conflict nonserializability.

examples.strategy: Build precedence edges only for same-item conflicts across different transactions.
examples.answer: The graph has a cycle, so the schedule is not conflict serializable.
examples.verification: Try serial T1,T2 and T2,T1: the former violates the Y constraint, the latter violates the X constraint. Commit/recovery properties are separate.

steps: The reads of X do not conflict.
W1(Y) before R2(Y) creates only \(T_1\to T_2\).
The graph is acyclic; serial order T1,T2 is conflict-equivalent.

pitfalls: Read-read overlap does not create a conflict.
Two-phase locking can still deadlock.
revision: WAL orders logging before corresponding data writes.

lessons.concept: Transactions group operations into a unit whose intermediate effects must be controlled. Concurrency can improve throughput, but interleavings must preserve an allowed relationship to serial execution and support recovery when work fails.
lessons.method:
A transaction groups operations into one logical unit. Atomicity makes its effects all succeed or all roll back; consistency preserves declared database invariants when transaction logic and enforcement are correct; isolation controls what concurrent executions can observe; durability retains committed effects after failures under the system’s guarantee.
These are different properties. A serial transaction can still violate an invariant if its logic is wrong, and durability does not prevent dirty reads. Logs and recovery mechanisms support atomicity/durability, while locks or other concurrency methods support isolation. Isolation levels may allow some anomalies, so do not equate every database’s default setting with full serializability.
A schedule interleaves transaction actions while preserving each transaction’s local order. Commit and abort mark outcomes; reading another transaction’s uncommitted write creates recovery risks. In GATE, identify which guarantee a failure scenario violates rather than choosing ACID as one undifferentiated label. An attempted operation and its durable committed result have distinct points in time. Conflicting actions belong to different transactions, access the same item and contain at least one write. Their order constrains any conflict-equivalent serial schedule. Create an edge Ti→Tj when Ti’s earlier conflicting action precedes Tj’s. The schedule is conflict serializable exactly when this directed graph is acyclic; a topological order supplies a serial witness.
Read/read pairs do not conflict, and actions on different items do not add edges. A cycle refutes conflict serializability, not every possible view-serializability notion. Blind writes can distinguish the two classes. Keep the transaction identities attached to each operation while scanning pairs.
Recovery tracks read-from dependencies and commit order, a separate question. If Tj reads Ti’s write, recoverability requires Ti commit before Tj commits. Cascadelessness forbids reading uncommitted writes; strictness also forbids overwriting them. A graph that is acyclic can still describe a recovery-unsafe execution if commits are ordered badly. Include commits when assessing those properties. Concurrency control coordinates simultaneous transactions to prevent disallowed anomalies. Two-phase locking divides a transaction into a growing phase with acquisitions and a shrinking phase with releases; after its first release it cannot acquire any new lock. Shared locks permit compatible reads, while exclusive locks protect conflicting writes under the lock table’s compatibility rules.
Basic 2PL guarantees conflict serializability but can deadlock and can permit recovery problems depending on release times. Strict 2PL holds exclusive locks until commit/abort, preventing other transactions from reading or overwriting those uncommitted protected writes. Holding all locks to completion is often called rigorous 2PL, so follow the problem’s terminology.
A transaction waiting for a lock must not proceed as though acquisition succeeded. Upgrades count as acquisitions and must respect the protocol. Alternative methods such as timestamp ordering or optimistic validation have different conflict handling. Atomicity gives all-or-nothing effects; consistency preserves declared invariants when transactions themselves are correct; isolation controls interference; durability preserves committed effects after recovery. Lost updates overwrite another transaction’s changes. Dirty reads observe uncommitted writes. Nonrepeatable reads and phantoms involve changing rows or predicate result sets across reads. Two operations conflict if they are in different transactions, access the same item, and at least one writes. Add Ti→Tj when Ti’s conflicting operation precedes Tj’s. The schedule is conflict serializable iff this precedence graph is acyclic; a topological order gives an equivalent serial ordering. Read-read pairs create no edge. Conflict serializability is stronger than some other semantic notions of serializability. Two-phase locking first acquires locks, then releases without acquiring new ones. It guarantees conflict serializability under the standard model but can deadlock. Strict variants retain required exclusive locks until commit/abort to prevent cascading effects. Write-ahead logging requires appropriate log records be durable before related dirty data pages are written. Recovery may redo committed work and undo uncommitted work according to its logging scheme. Conflict ordering constrains transactions when actions from different transactions touch the same item and at least one is a write. Read/read order adds no conflict edge. Two-phase locking forbids new lock acquisitions after the first release and guarantees conflict serializability, but can deadlock.
