method: For the precedence graph connect different transactions when conflicting same-item actions occur in order.
Acyclicity gives a conflict-equivalent serial order via topological sorting.
For recovery track who read whose uncommitted write and compare commit order; distinguish basic, strict and rigorous 2PL.

traps.claim: Every serializable schedule is recoverable
traps.why: T2 can read T1’s write and commit before T1 aborts even if the conflict order is serializable.

traps.claim: Every cycle proves lack of view serializability
traps.why: It disproves conflict serializability; blind writes can permit view-serializable schedules outside that class.

formulas.meaning: An earlier conflicting action of Ti precedes an action of Tj on the same item; at least one is a write.
Recoverability requires writer Ti to commit before reader Tj commits when Tj reads Ti’s value.

tutorials.title: Transactions and the ACID guarantees
tutorials.body:
A transaction groups operations into one logical unit. Atomicity makes its effects all succeed or all roll back; consistency preserves declared database invariants when transaction logic and enforcement are correct; isolation controls what concurrent executions can observe; durability retains committed effects after failures under the system’s guarantee.
These are different properties. A serial transaction can still violate an invariant if its logic is wrong, and durability does not prevent dirty reads. Logs and recovery mechanisms support atomicity/durability, while locks or other concurrency methods support isolation. Isolation levels may allow some anomalies, so do not equate every database’s default setting with full serializability.
A schedule interleaves transaction actions while preserving each transaction’s local order. Commit and abort mark outcomes; reading another transaction’s uncommitted write creates recovery risks. In GATE, identify which guarantee a failure scenario violates rather than choosing ACID as one undifferentiated label. An attempted operation and its durable committed result have distinct points in time.

example.prompt: A transfer subtracts 100 from account A, then crashes before adding it to B.
example.strategy: Partial effects → Atomicity requirement → Recovery outcome

steps.title: Partial effects
steps.explanation: Without recovery, total balance drops even though the intended transfer did not complete.

steps.title: Atomicity requirement
steps.explanation: Both debit and credit must be treated as one unit, completed or undone.

steps.title: Recovery outcome
steps.explanation: An uncommitted partial transfer should be rolled back under the stated atomicity mechanism.

example.answer: Atomicity addresses the partial-transaction failure.
example.verification: Durability instead concerns retaining a transfer that had already successfully committed.

tutorials.title: Conflict graphs, recoverability and commit order
tutorials.body:
Conflicting actions belong to different transactions, access the same item and contain at least one write. Their order constrains any conflict-equivalent serial schedule. Create an edge Ti→Tj when Ti’s earlier conflicting action precedes Tj’s. The schedule is conflict serializable exactly when this directed graph is acyclic; a topological order supplies a serial witness.
Read/read pairs do not conflict, and actions on different items do not add edges. A cycle refutes conflict serializability, not every possible view-serializability notion. Blind writes can distinguish the two classes. Keep the transaction identities attached to each operation while scanning pairs.
Recovery tracks read-from dependencies and commit order, a separate question. If Tj reads Ti’s write, recoverability requires Ti commit before Tj commits. Cascadelessness forbids reading uncommitted writes; strictness also forbids overwriting them. A graph that is acyclic can still describe a recovery-unsafe execution if commits are ordered badly. Include commits when assessing those properties.

example.prompt: Schedule W1(X),R2(X),W2(Y),R1(Y).
example.strategy: Conflict on X → Conflict on Y → Cycle

steps.title: Conflict on X
steps.explanation: W1 before R2 imposes \(T_1\to T_2\).

steps.title: Conflict on Y
steps.explanation: W2 before R1 imposes \(T_2\to T_1\).

steps.title: Cycle
steps.explanation: The two edges form a directed cycle, so no serial order respects both.

example.answer: Not conflict serializable.
example.verification: This conclusion does not need commit times, while recoverability would require read-from and commit/abort information.

tutorials.title: Two-phase locking and strictness
tutorials.body:
Concurrency control coordinates simultaneous transactions to prevent disallowed anomalies. Two-phase locking divides a transaction into a growing phase with acquisitions and a shrinking phase with releases; after its first release it cannot acquire any new lock. Shared locks permit compatible reads, while exclusive locks protect conflicting writes under the lock table’s compatibility rules.
Basic 2PL guarantees conflict serializability but can deadlock and can permit recovery problems depending on release times. Strict 2PL holds exclusive locks until commit/abort, preventing other transactions from reading or overwriting those uncommitted protected writes. Holding all locks to completion is often called rigorous 2PL, so follow the problem’s terminology.
A transaction waiting for a lock must not proceed as though acquisition succeeded. Upgrades count as acquisitions and must respect the protocol. Alternative methods such as timestamp ordering or optimistic validation have different conflict handling. In GATE traces, test both phase ordering and compatibility; a serializable particular schedule need not mean every listed protocol rule was followed.

example.prompt: T1 acquires X, releases X, then requests Y. Does it obey basic 2PL?
example.strategy: Growing phase → Begin shrinking → Later request

steps.title: Growing phase
steps.explanation: The first acquisition is permitted.

steps.title: Begin shrinking
steps.explanation: Releasing X ends the period in which new acquisitions are allowed.

steps.title: Later request
steps.explanation: Acquiring Y afterward violates the two-phase rule.

example.answer: It violates 2PL.
example.verification: The prohibition is about phase order, even if no other transaction currently holds Y.

lessons.title: Layering, switching and network performance
lessons.intuition: A network separates services into layers so each solves a manageable part of delivery. Packets share infrastructure, while circuits reserve capacity. Delay depends on several physical and queueing effects, so bandwidth and latency are not interchangeable.

sections.title: Layers and encapsulation
sections.body: An application message becomes transport data, then a network packet, then a link frame under common Internet layering. Each layer adds addressing/control information appropriate to its scope. A router forwards network-layer packets; a typical Ethernet switch forwards link-layer frames. End-to-end services and per-link services solve different problems.

sections.title: Switching models
sections.body: Circuit switching reserves a route or channel allocation, potentially with setup overhead and unused reserved capacity. Packet switching shares links among packets and can queue under load. Datagram packets can be routed independently; a virtual circuit establishes logical forwarding state before transfer, typically using a label on subsequent packets. A logical virtual circuit is not necessarily a physically reserved circuit.

sections.title: Delay and throughput
sections.body: Transmission delay=L/R for L bits on rate R; propagation delay=distance/signal speed. Processing and queueing add further delay. Store-and-forward requires a full packet before forwarding in the basic model. Bottleneck link rate constrains sustained throughput. With multiple packets and links, serialization can be pipelined; don’t multiply entire end-to-end latency by packet count automatically.

sections.title: Serialization, propagation and pipeline overlap
sections.body: A link serializes a packet by placing its bits onto the medium over L/R seconds. Once a bit is launched, propagation carries it across the link over distance/speed seconds. Doubling packet length doubles serialization but does not change an individual bit’s propagation delay. A store-and-forward router must receive the complete packet before starting its outgoing serialization. Across equal-rate links, successive packets can overlap on different links; the first packet pays the full path serialization, while later packets emerge at the bottleneck packet interval under the simplified no-queuing model. Routers replace link-layer framing for the next hop while forwarding toward the network-layer destination. Circuit setup and reserved capacity belong to a different service model than ordinary statistical multiplexing.

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: Convert to bits: \(1500\cdot8=12000\). The rate is given in bits per second, so leaving packet size in bytes would undercount time by a factor of eight.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: Transmission delay=\(\frac{12000}{12\cdot10^6}=0.001\) s. Mbps uses decimal millions here; the resulting quotient is in seconds.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: That is 1 ms, excluding propagation and queueing. This calculation concerns serialization only. Distance or router delays cannot be inferred from packet size and link rate alone.

examples.strategy: Convert packet bytes to bits, then divide by bit rate.
examples.answer: That is 1 ms, excluding propagation and queueing.
examples.verification: 12,000 bits at 12,000,000 bits/s is 1/1000 s=1 ms, with consistent dimensions.

examples.prompt: Two store-and-forward links at the same rate, no other delay
steps: The first packet needs one transmission time on each link, total 2t.
For N packets, after the first link finishes one it can send the next while the next link forwards the previous.
Completion is (N+1)t for two equal links under these assumptions, not 2Nt.

pitfalls: Convert bytes to bits before dividing by bit rate.
Faster bandwidth does not reduce propagation distance.

checks.prompt: A 1000-byte packet uses an 8 Mbps link. What is transmission delay in milliseconds?
checks.hint: Convert bytes to bits.

checks.prompt: Propagation distance is 600 km and speed 200000 km/s. What is propagation delay in milliseconds?
checks.hint: Divide distance by speed and convert seconds.

Separate serialization from propagation, queuing and processing.

traps.claim: Propagation delay grows with packet size
traps.why: It depends on distance and propagation speed; serialization depends on packet length and link rate.

traps.claim: Every layer uses the same destination address
traps.why: Link destination is normally the next hop; network destination usually remains the remote host.

formulas.meaning: L bits at R bits/s.
Distance d and signal speed s in consistent units.

example.prompt: A host sends to a remote host via a router on the local Ethernet.

steps.title: Network destination

steps.title: Router forwarding

steps.title: First packet
steps.explanation: It exits link one at t and link two at 2t.

steps.title: Overlap
steps.explanation: Link one sends packet two while link two sends packet one.

steps.title: Final completion
steps.explanation: Packets two and three then exit at 3t and 4t.

lessons.title: Error detection, MAC and Ethernet
lessons.prerequisite: Binary polynomials, frames and shared media.
lessons.intuition: The link layer moves frames over one link and manages its local addressing and error checks. Error detection identifies some corrupt frames; it is not automatically error correction. Shared-medium access rules matter only where senders actually contend for the same medium.

sections.title: Parity, checksums and CRC
sections.body: A parity bit detects any odd number of bit flips but can miss an even number. Internet-style checksums use one’s-complement arithmetic. CRC treats bits as polynomial coefficients over GF(2): addition/subtraction is XOR. Append r zeros for a degree-r generator, divide, and append the r-bit remainder. A receiver divides the received codeword; a nonzero remainder detects an error.

sections.title: Medium access
sections.body: ALOHA transmits with probabilistic contention; carrier-sense protocols listen before transmitting. Classic half-duplex Ethernet uses CSMA/CD, detecting collisions and backing off. The minimum frame time must support collision detection over the collision domain under its physical assumptions. Full-duplex switched Ethernet has separate bidirectional links and does not use collision detection.

sections.title: Ethernet switching
sections.body: MAC addresses identify local link interfaces. A learning switch records the source MAC and ingress port. Known destination addresses are forwarded to the corresponding port; unknown destinations and relevant broadcasts are flooded according to VLAN/topology rules. Routers separate network-layer domains; a link switch does not usually choose routes by IP prefix.

sections.title: Why sequence-space bounds prevent ambiguity
sections.body: A sender may have multiple frames outstanding while acknowledgments are delayed. Sequence numbers wrap, so a delayed old frame must not be mistaken for a new frame with the same number. Selective repeat accepts and buffers a window of out-of-order frames; disjoint old and new windows require the usual half-sequence-space bound. Go-back-N’s receiver ordinarily accepts only the next expected frame, yielding a different maximum sender window. State those receiver models before using memorized bounds. CRC treats bitstrings as polynomials over GF(2), so subtraction is XOR without borrow. Appending r zeros multiplies data by xʳ; the division remainder produces a codeword divisible by the generator. Detection guarantees depend on the error polynomial and generator, not just the remainder’s length.

examples.prompt: Detect a single flipped bit with even parity

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: Suppose data has an even number of 1s and parity bit 0. The sender chooses the parity bit so the complete protected word has an even number of ones.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: One flipped bit changes overall parity to odd. One bit flip changes the number of ones by plus or minus one, which reverses its parity.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: The receiver detects mismatch, but cannot locate the bad bit from parity alone. Mismatch reports inconsistency but does not identify which of the possible bit positions changed.

examples.strategy: Evaluate parity detection separately from correction capability.
examples.answer: The receiver detects mismatch, but cannot locate the bad bit from parity alone.
examples.verification: Two flipped bits can restore even parity and escape detection; the result is a single-bit detection guarantee, not an arbitrary-error guarantee.

steps: Generator degree is 3, so divide appended data 1001000 by 1011 using XOR.
First XOR gives 0010000; align again and XOR to get 0000110.
Remainder is 110; transmit 1001110. Dividing this codeword by 1011 gives zero remainder.

pitfalls: CRC division uses XOR without carries.
Modern full-duplex Ethernet does not use CSMA/CD.
revision: Degree-r CRC appends r check bits.
Switch learns source MAC, forwards by destination MAC.

checks.hint: One flip changes parity.
checks.explanation: The single parity check fails once; it detects but does not locate the error.

tutorials.title: CRC polynomial division without carries
tutorials.body:
CRC interprets a bit string as a polynomial over GF(2), where addition/subtraction are XOR. A generator of degree r requires r check bits. Append r zero bits to the data, divide by the generator using aligned XOR, and attach the resulting r-bit remainder to the original data. The transmitted codeword then divides with zero remainder.
At reception, a nonzero remainder detects inconsistency. An error whose polynomial is divisible by the generator can evade detection, so exact guarantees depend on generator factors and error length. The conventional nonzero constant term ensures relevant trailing behavior. CRC is normally detection, not automatic correction.
Write each XOR alignment rather than using decimal integer division or subtraction with borrows. A generator’s bit length is r+1, while remainder width is r. Keep leading zeros in that remainder to preserve field width. GATE examples may ask the codeword, remainder or whether a supplied error pattern is detected; these are related but not identical tasks.

tutorials.title: Shared-medium access and Ethernet duplex assumptions
tutorials.body:
Medium access control coordinates transmitters sharing a channel. ALOHA transmits with limited coordination and retries collisions; carrier-sense methods first inspect activity. Classic half-duplex shared Ethernet uses CSMA/CD, detecting collisions while sending and backing off. The minimum frame-time reasoning ensures distant collisions can still be observed before transmission ends.
Modern switched full-duplex Ethernet separates transmit/receive paths and does not use classic collision detection on those links. A switch learns source link addresses and forwards frames according to its table, flooding when a destination is unknown under ordinary behavior. This is different from an IP router’s longest-prefix decision.
State topology, duplex and link rate before applying a shared-bus formula. Wireless collision avoidance uses different assumptions from collision detection, since hearing the channel does not guarantee the receiver sees no interference. GATE distinctions often test whether CSMA/CD applies to every Ethernet situation. Link-layer addressing and frame checks still exist in full duplex even though shared-medium collisions do not.

lessons.title: Distance-vector and link-state routing
lessons.prerequisite: Graphs, shortest paths and link costs.
lessons.intuition: Routers need a distributed way to learn where to send packets. Distance-vector exchanges route estimates with neighbours; link-state distributes topology so each router can compute routes locally. The information each approach shares explains its failure modes.

sections.title: Distance-vector update
sections.body: A router x estimates Dx(y)=minᵥ[c(x,v)+Dv(y)] over neighbours v. Each advertisement supplies a neighbour’s current estimate. Updates may be asynchronous and transient inconsistencies arise when links fail. A destination that becomes unreachable may have increasing estimates passed around, producing count-to-infinity.

sections.title: Mitigations and link-state
sections.body: Split horizon avoids advertising a route back on the interface from which it was learned; poisoned reverse explicitly advertises an infinite metric in that direction. These do not solve every possible loop topology. Link-state routers discover neighbours/costs, flood sequenced link-state advertisements and run Dijkstra on their assembled topology. Sequence numbers and aging prevent stale information from circulating indefinitely.

sections.title: Forwarding versus routing
sections.body: Routing computes and updates the control-plane table; forwarding uses it for individual packets. A next hop need not be the destination itself. Correct convergence is distinct from instantaneous consistency during updates. Compare control traffic, stored knowledge and recovery behaviour rather than assuming one protocol is universally superior.

sections.title: Local advertisements versus global topology
sections.body: A distance-vector router stores estimates learned from neighbors and chooses the neighbor minimizing link cost plus advertised remaining distance. If a neighbor’s route actually depends on the router itself, stale messages after a failure can create a loop. Split horizon and poison reverse suppress some immediate feedback, but are not universal proofs against every multi-router convergence problem. Link-state routers flood link information so each can compute from a topology snapshot; inconsistent or old snapshots can still produce transient behavior. After routes are installed, forwarding chooses among destination prefixes by longest match. A more specific route overrides a broader matching route even if the broader one appears first or has a lower cost metric; route selection within a prefix and forwarding specificity are separate stages.

lessons.title: IPv4, CIDR and network address translation
lessons.intuition: An IPv4 address contains 32 bits. CIDR says how many leading bits define the routing prefix. NAT rewrites selected addresses and ports, often allowing several private hosts to share a public address, but it changes end-to-end addressing assumptions.

sections.title: CIDR arithmetic
sections.body: A /p prefix leaves 32−p varying bits and contains 2^(32−p) total addresses. In conventional multiaccess subnets, network and broadcast addresses are not assignable hosts, giving two fewer; /31 point-to-point and /32 cases require different treatment. Masking an address with the subnet mask gives its network prefix. Block boundaries follow the mask, not arbitrary decimal rounding.

sections.title: Longest-prefix match
sections.body: A packet destination may match several routes. Select the matching route with the largest prefix length, because it identifies the most specific region. The default /0 matches everything but loses to any more-specific match. A route’s prefix need not match a classful address boundary; CIDR replaced that restriction.

sections.title: NAT/PAT
sections.body: Address translation rewrites private/public addresses; port translation distinguishes multiple internal transport sessions sharing an external IP. The device keeps mappings and updates required checksums. Incoming connections need a mapping or explicit forwarding arrangement. NAT is not equivalent to a complete security policy and can complicate protocols embedding addresses in payloads.

sections.title: Bits determine alignment and aggregation
sections.body: A /p prefix fixes the first p address bits and leaves 32−p host bits. The network address sets those remaining bits to zero; under ordinary subnet semantics the directed broadcast sets them all to one. A /26 leaves six bits, so last-octet boundaries occur at multiples of 64. Aggregating two /p blocks into /p−1 is valid only if their prefixes differ in the last prefix bit and share all earlier bits. Numerically adjacent blocks can cross an alignment boundary and fail this test. Conventional host-count subtraction reserves network and broadcast addresses, but /31 point-to-point addressing and /32 host routes use different conventions. Private addressing, NAT and CIDR solve different needs: a private address is not itself a routing prefix-length rule.

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: There are 6 host bits, so blocks contain 64 addresses. Prefix length 26 leaves 32−26=6 host bits, giving 64 total addresses per block.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: The last-octet ranges begin 0,64,128,192; 70 lies in 64–127. Integer division of the final octet by 64 identifies its block: floor(70/64)=1, beginning at 64.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: Network is 192.168.1.64, conventional broadcast .127, with hosts .65–.126. Under conventional subnet semantics the first and last addresses are network and broadcast; they are excluded from the host range.

examples.strategy: Find the aligned CIDR block by host-bit width and boundary multiples.
examples.answer: Network is 192.168.1.64, conventional broadcast .127, with hosts .65–.126.
examples.verification: 70 AND 192 gives 64 in the last octet. The host range contains 62 addresses, from 65 through 126 inclusive.

lessons.title: IPv4 fragmentation step by step
lessons.prerequisite: IPv4 headers, byte counts and division.
lessons.intuition: An IP datagram may exceed a link’s maximum transmission unit. Fragmentation divides its payload while preserving enough information to reassemble at the destination. Headers are repeated for every fragment, and offsets locate payload bytes rather than whole datagram bytes.

sections.title: Payload capacity
sections.body: MTU limits the total IP fragment length including its own IP header. With header H, payload capacity is MTU−H. Every nonfinal fragment payload must be a multiple of 8 bytes, so use floor((MTU−H)/8)×8 when creating maximal nonfinal fragments. The final payload may be smaller and need not be an eight-byte multiple.

sections.title: Header interpretation
sections.body: Fragments share the relevant source,destination,protocol and identification association. The fragment offset measures where this payload starts in the original payload, in units of 8 bytes. MF=1 says more fragments follow; MF=0 identifies the final portion, not necessarily a complete unfragmented original. DF forbids fragmentation, so an oversize packet must be handled by failure/feedback under the protocol instead.

sections.title: Reassembly reasoning
sections.body: Add payload lengths to verify the original payload total. Calculate offsets cumulatively from payload, excluding repeated headers. IPv4 permits routers to fragment when allowed; destination reassembly handles the pieces. Loss of one needed fragment prevents normal complete delivery of the original datagram, adding a reason large fragmented packets can be fragile.

sections.title: Offsets describe the original payload
sections.body: Each fragment is a separate IP packet with its own header and total length. The offset identifies where its data belongs in the original IP payload; counting previous fragment headers would misplace reassembly. Nonfinal payload sizes must be multiples of eight because the next offset has eight-byte granularity. The last payload may have a remainder. Fragmentation adds header overhead, so summed transmitted fragment lengths exceed original length when more than one fragment is produced. Identification, source, destination and protocol help associate fragments; offset and MF locate the payload boundaries. If an already fragmented packet is fragmented again, offsets remain relative to the original payload, and a piece that is last only within its parent fragment can still require MF=1. IPv6 routers do not perform the same in-network fragmentation process as IPv4 routers.

examples.prompt: Fragment a 4000-byte datagram with 20-byte header across MTU 1500

steps.title: Separate header from payload
steps.explanation: The original total length includes one header. Headers added to fragments are not part of the original payload offsets.

steps.title: Find the nonfinal capacity

lessons.title: TCP flow/congestion control, sockets, DNS and HTTP
lessons.intuition: TCP transports an ordered byte stream using sequence numbers, acknowledgments and retransmission. The receiver’s capacity and the network’s capacity are separate limits. Application protocols then interpret those delivered bytes or use other transport mechanisms.

sections.title: Reliability and windows
sections.body: TCP sequence numbers refer to bytes, and cumulative acknowledgments identify the next expected byte under the usual model. A receive window rwnd advertises buffering capacity. A congestion window cwnd estimates what the sender should inject into the network. The usable limit is approximately min(rwnd,cwnd) minus bytes already outstanding, subject to further implementation rules.

sections.title: Congestion control
sections.body: In the classical teaching model, slow start grows cwnd roughly exponentially per RTT until a threshold or loss indication. Congestion avoidance grows more slowly, often about one MSS per RTT. Timeout and duplicate-ACK loss reactions differ across variants; read the specified algorithm. Bandwidth-delay product estimates data needed in flight to keep a path busy; a too-small window limits throughput.

sections.title: Sockets, DNS and HTTP
sections.body: A TCP server commonly socket/bind/listen/accepts; a client connects, then both send/receive a byte stream without preserved message boundaries. DNS maps names and other records through hierarchy and caches, commonly using UDP but also TCP. HTTP defines methods, status codes, headers and message semantics. Persistent connections reuse transport. HTTP/3 runs over QUIC/UDP, so do not assume every HTTP version uses TCP.

sections.title: Track byte intervals and independent windows
sections.body: A segment with sequence s and b data bytes covers the inclusive byte interval s through s+b−1. If all earlier bytes have arrived, the cumulative ACK is s+b, the next expected byte. Out-of-order arrival need not advance that ACK across a gap. SYN and FIN each consume sequence-number space even without application data. The receive window advertises buffer availability; congestion window is a sender-side network-control quantity. New sending allowance is the smaller window minus bytes already outstanding, bounded below by zero. A large window alone does not guarantee its window/RTT throughput bound is attained: bottleneck link rate, loss, application supply and startup can constrain it further. Retransmission, flow control and congestion control must be tracked as separate mechanisms.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: Additional permissible in-flight data is \(10000-4000=6000\) bytes in the simplified model. New data allowance is unused window capacity, not the entire window. A negative result would mean no new data can be sent.

lessons.title: The socket API and TCP byte-stream framing
lessons.intuition: A socket is a programming interface to network communication. Establishing a connection and exchanging application messages are separate tasks. TCP delivers a byte stream, so the application must decide how to recognize message boundaries.

sections.title: Server lifecycle
sections.body: Create a socket, bind it to a local address/port, listen for incoming connections and accept. accept returns a connected socket for one peer while the listening socket remains for future connections. A server can serve multiple clients using threads, processes or nonblocking/event-driven I/O. Privileged-port and address-binding rules depend on the OS.

sections.title: Client and data transfer
sections.body: A TCP client creates a socket and calls connect to the server endpoint. send/recv may transfer fewer bytes than requested; robust code loops as needed. A recv returning zero for a TCP stream indicates an orderly peer closure after available data is exhausted. Errors and timeouts need handling rather than assuming every operation completes immediately.

sections.title: Application framing
sections.body: One send call need not equal one recv call. Define a length prefix, delimiter with escaping, fixed record size or another protocol framing scheme. Accumulate incoming bytes until one complete message is available, retain surplus bytes for the next message, and bound lengths to avoid unbounded allocation. Network byte order converts multibyte integer fields consistently.

sections.title: Message framing over a byte stream
sections.body: TCP supplies reliable ordered bytes but no boundary markers between application writes. A sender can write a length header and payload separately, while a receiver gets a combined chunk, a partial header or a partial payload. A correct receive loop accumulates enough bytes for the agreed header, validates the declared length, then accumulates exactly that many payload bytes. Remaining bytes may belong to the next message and should not be discarded. A return of zero conventionally indicates orderly end of stream, which differs from a short positive read. A listening TCP socket accepts multiple connections into separate connected sockets. UDP preserves datagram boundaries under its API but does not add TCP’s ordered delivery/retransmission guarantees; an application must choose its own reliability semantics.

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: Encode length 5 in the agreed prefix format. Both peers must agree on prefix size, byte order and length semantics before interpreting payload bytes.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: Transmit the prefix and five payload bytes, allowing for partial writes. A short positive write sends only part of the buffer; continue from the first unsent byte rather than retransmitting already sent bytes.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: The receiver first accumulates the complete prefix, then exactly five payload bytes, even if several recv calls are needed. The receiver accumulates exactly the declared payload length. A short read does not indicate the message ended.

lessons.title: DNS hierarchy, resolution and caching
lessons.intuition: DNS distributes naming information across a hierarchy rather than storing every name in one central server. Resolution may require several queries, but caching avoids repeating most of that work until records expire.

sections.title: Names and authority
sections.body: A domain name is a sequence of labels. Root servers direct queries toward relevant top-level-domain servers, which direct them toward authoritative servers for delegated zones. An authoritative answer describes data in that zone; a recursive resolver acts for a client and obtains/caches answers. Delegation boundaries and host labels are not interchangeable concepts.

sections.title: Query behaviour
sections.body: In recursive resolution, the requester asks a resolver to return a final answer or failure. The resolver can use iterative queries, following referrals rather than asking each upstream server to do the whole lookup. Cached records have TTL lifetimes. Caching both answers and referrals can reduce later queries; a cached IP may expire before or after related delegation records.

sections.title: Records and transport
sections.body: A records map names to IPv4 addresses; AAAA to IPv6; CNAME expresses aliases; MX identifies mail exchangers; NS identifies name servers. DNS commonly uses UDP port 53 for ordinary queries and can use TCP, including for larger/truncated responses and zone transfers under their relevant rules. DNS is not always UDP, and a domain can map to more than one address.

sections.title: Delegation and caches change the query path
sections.body: The root directs a resolver toward a top-level-domain authority, which can direct it toward an authoritative server for a narrower zone. These are referrals, not necessarily the final host address. A recursive resolver performs this work on behalf of its client; iterative exchanges supply answers or referrals one step at a time. Cached answers and delegation records have separate TTLs, so a cache can skip some exchanges but still need an authoritative lookup. A CNAME is an alias whose target may require further resolution; MX selects mail-exchanger names, not automatically their numeric IP addresses. Delay counting should identify which requests are serial and which cached records exist at the start. lessons.concept: DNS distributes naming information across a hierarchy rather than storing every name in one central server. Resolution may require several queries, but caching avoids repeating most of that work until records expire.
lessons.method:
DNS maps names to typed resource records in a delegated hierarchy. A client stub often asks a recursive resolver to obtain the final answer. That resolver may query root, top-level-domain and authoritative servers as needed, receiving referrals or answers. In an iterative exchange, a server supplies what it knows and the requester follows the next referral.
Recursive versus iterative describes who performs the remaining resolution work; it is not simply whether “many packets” are used. Cached answers and delegation records can skip levels, so every lookup need not contact root. An authoritative answer comes from the responsible zone, while a cached response can still be valid without that server contact.
DNS commonly uses UDP but also TCP and other transports, so not every response is one small UDP packet. A CNAME target may require additional resolution. GATE delay counting should identify cache state, serial query exchanges and any parallel operations. A referral to another nameserver is not automatically the requested host’s numeric address. Resource records specify a name, type, class, TTL and type-dependent data. A holds an IPv4 address, AAAA an IPv6 address, NS names an authoritative/delegated server, MX names a mail exchanger with preference, and CNAME makes an alias to another name. The record type determines what the data means; an MX name is not already its numeric IP address.
TTL bounds how long a cached record can be reused under ordinary expiry handling. Remaining lifetime decreases with elapsed time and is not renewed simply because a client reads it. An authoritative new response can provide fresh information. Different cached records in one resolution path can have different lifetimes.
Negative caching and additional-section data follow protocol rules rather than a blanket “cache everything forever.” For GATE arithmetic, state no refresh/eviction and subtract age from TTL, not from wall-clock midnight. For alias traces, follow the target until the requested record is found and avoid treating an alias label as the address. DNS naming does not itself establish a transport connection to the resulting service. A domain name is a sequence of labels. Root servers direct queries toward relevant top-level-domain servers, which direct them toward authoritative servers for delegated zones. An authoritative answer describes data in that zone; a recursive resolver acts for a client and obtains/caches answers. Delegation boundaries and host labels are not interchangeable concepts. In recursive resolution, the requester asks a resolver to return a final answer or failure. The resolver can use iterative queries, following referrals rather than asking each upstream server to do the whole lookup. Cached records have TTL lifetimes. Caching both answers and referrals can reduce later queries; a cached IP may expire before or after related delegation records. A records map names to IPv4 addresses; AAAA to IPv6; CNAME expresses aliases; MX identifies mail exchangers; NS identifies name servers. DNS commonly uses UDP port 53 for ordinary queries and can use TCP, including for larger/truncated responses and zone transfers under their relevant rules. DNS is not always UDP, and a domain can map to more than one address. The root directs a resolver toward a top-level-domain authority, which can direct it toward an authoritative server for a narrower zone. These are referrals, not necessarily the final host address. A recursive resolver performs this work on behalf of its client; iterative exchanges supply answers or referrals one step at a time. Cached answers and delegation records have separate TTLs, so a cache can skip some exchanges but still need an authoritative lookup. A CNAME is an alias whose target may require further resolution; MX selects mail-exchanger names, not automatically their numeric IP addresses. Delay counting should identify which requests are serial and which cached records exist at the start. UDP is common for queries, but TCP and other DNS transports also exist; protocol correctness is not equivalent to a single UDP exchange.

lessons.title: HTTP requests, responses and persistent connections
lessons.intuition: HTTP defines application-level meaning: which resource is requested, what action is asked for and how the response is described. Its semantics are separate from the transport connection and remain recognizable across protocol versions.

sections.title: Request and response structure
sections.body: A request carries a method, target and headers, often with a body. GET retrieves a representation; POST commonly submits processing data; PUT replaces at a known target under its semantics. A response includes a status code, headers and possibly a body. Status classes 2xx indicate success, 3xx redirection, 4xx client-side request problems and 5xx server-side failures.

sections.title: Persistence and latency
sections.body: Persistent connections reuse transport for multiple requests, reducing repeated setup. HTTP/1.1 generally supports persistent connections; HTTP/2 multiplexes streams within its transport model. HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP rather than TCP. A latency question must specify DNS/cache state, connection establishment, transfer size, request dependencies and whether connections can be reused.

sections.title: Caching and security
sections.body: Cache-Control and related metadata control reuse; conditional requests can validate existing content rather than redownload it. HTTPS protects HTTP exchange using the applicable secure transport, but does not change what GET or a status code means. An HTTP cache and a DNS cache store different information and can have unrelated expiry times.

sections.title: Build an explicit latency model
sections.body: For one object over a fresh TCP connection, a simplified model counts one RTT for establishment and one RTT for the request and start of response, then object transmission. It omits DNS, TLS, congestion startup and queuing unless supplied. Persistence reuses the connection and avoids repeating setup. HTTP/1.1 without pipelining can still issue requests sequentially; HTTP/2 multiplexes streams over a connection; HTTP/3 uses QUIC streams over UDP. Cache freshness can avoid a network request, while conditional validation still contacts the server and may receive 304 rather than a complete body. An HTTP error status is a valid application response; connection refusal occurs before such a response. Any numerical RTT answer must specify connection reuse, parallel connections and which transfers overlap.

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: The server produced a valid protocol response. Receiving an HTTP status line implies that an application-level response was exchanged over an established transport.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: Its status is in the 4xx category and indicates the requested resource was not found under the response semantics. 404 concerns the requested resource, not the inability to contact the server at all.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: This is not the same as a TCP connection refusal, where no HTTP exchange may have occurred. Connection refusal prevents the request/response exchange; retrying it is a different diagnostic path from inspecting a 404 URL.

examples.answer: This is not the same as a TCP connection refusal, where no HTTP exchange may have occurred.

lessons.title: Quantitative aptitude: ratios, percentages and work
lessons.intuition: Quantitative aptitude usually rewards a clean model rather than lengthy computation. Define units and the reference quantity first. A percentage is relative to a base; a work time converts to a rate before people working together can be combined.

sections.title: Ratios and averages
sections.body: If A:B=a:b, write A=ak and B=bk. This preserves the relationship while totals determine k. A weighted average is total weighted value divided by total weight, not the unweighted average of subgroup averages. Check whether group sizes are equal before averaging percentages.

sections.title: Successive changes
sections.body: Increase by p% multiplies by 1+p/100; decrease by q% multiplies by 1−q/100. Combine multipliers to find overall change. Equal percentage rises and falls do not cancel because their bases differ. Profit percentage uses cost price as its base unless explicitly redefined.

sections.title: Work and speed
sections.body: A worker completing one job in t days works at 1/t jobs per day under constant-rate assumptions. Independent rates add for shared work; time is reciprocal total rate. Distance=rate×time with consistent units. Relative speed adds for opposite travel directions and subtracts for same-direction catch-up.

steps.title: Apply the increase
steps.explanation: The first percentage has base 100.

steps.title: Apply the decrease to its actual base
steps.explanation: The second percentage has base 120. Its absolute decrease is 24, larger than the original increase 20.

steps.title: Measure change relative to the original
steps.explanation: Net percentage must use the initial value as denominator, not 120 or 96.

examples.goal: Find final value and net percentage change.
examples.strategy: Apply each percentage to its current base, using multiplication rather than subtracting percentages.

lessons.method:
A percentage is a fraction of a specified base. An increase by p% multiplies the current quantity by 1+p/100; a decrease multiplies by 1−p/100. Sequential changes use the updated base, so equal rise/fall percentages do not cancel. Percentage points describe the arithmetic difference between two percentages, not a relative percent change.
Reverse a percentage by dividing by its multiplier, not subtracting the same percentage from the final quantity. Profit/cost and discount/marked-price questions can use different bases even within one sentence. Write the named base beside every step before calculating.
A useful check is whether the numerical result matches direction and magnitude: a 10% rise must add one tenth of the original, not leave only that tenth. For equal fractional rise/fall r, final multiplier is 1−r². Quantitative aptitude also rewards translating a verbal condition into a short equation before testing options. Keep exact fractions where possible, and apply rounding only at the end. A ratio a:b states relative magnitudes, not actual values. Represent two quantities as ak and bk with one common scale k. If their total is T, k=T/(a+b); if a difference is given use the difference of coefficients. Ratios can compare different units only after consistent conversion or with their dimensional meaning clearly retained.
Combine ratios through a common shared quantity: for A:B and B:C, scale both so B’s coefficients agree. Directly appending unrelated coefficients gives the wrong combined proportion. Weighted averages multiply each subgroup’s value by its weight/count and divide by total weight; averaging two subgroup averages without weights assumes equal subgroup sizes.
A change in one component can alter both numerator and denominator of a ratio. Define unknowns and translate the new condition before solving. For GATE, test the resulting quantities in the original ratio and the total/difference equation. An exact rational answer is often easier to verify than early decimal rounding, particularly in mixture and speed problems. For a constant-rate worker completing one job in t time units, rate is 1/t jobs per unit time. Independent workers on the same divisible job add rates, not durations. The reciprocal of total rate gives total completion time. If efficiencies vary, work stops or workers interfere, model those changes rather than assuming the simple independent formula.
Travel uses distance=speed×time. Average speed is total distance/total time; an arithmetic average of speeds is valid for equal times, while equal-distance legs use the harmonic expression 2v₁v₂/(v₁+v₂). Convert units before addition or division. A “negative worker” such as a drain subtracts rate under a constant-rate model.

Accumulated work is sum of rate×duration on each interval and cannot exceed the required job before a phase change is reached. GATE aptitude options often exploit averaging times rather than rates. A weighted average is total weighted value divided by total weight, not the unweighted average of subgroup averages. Check whether group sizes are equal before averaging percentages. Profit percentage uses cost price as its base unless explicitly redefined. A worker completing one job in t days works at 1/t jobs per day under constant-rate assumptions. Independent rates add for shared work; time is reciprocal total rate. Distance=rate×time with consistent units. Relative speed adds for opposite travel directions and subtracts for same-direction catch-up.

Make a table of rates and active time intervals for workers joining/leaving. Accumulated work is sum of rate×duration on each interval and cannot exceed the required job before a phase change is reached. GATE aptitude options often exploit averaging times rather than rates. Check whether a combined faster rate yields a time smaller than either worker’s solo time.

example.prompt: A finishes in 6 days, B in 3. They work together under constant independent rates.
example.strategy: Individual rates → Combine → Time

steps.title: Individual rates
steps.explanation: Use jobs per day.

steps.title: Combine
steps.explanation: The same total job receives both contributions.

steps.title: Time
steps.explanation: Invert the combined rate.

example.answer: Two days.
example.verification: A does 2/6 of the job and B 2/3; the contributions sum to one.

lessons.title: Verbal, analytical and spatial aptitude
lessons.prerequisite: Reading comprehension and careful constraint tracking.
lessons.intuition: Reasoning tasks ask you to respect exactly the available evidence. In verbal problems, grammatical role and meaning constrain the answer; in arrangements, each clue reduces the allowed states. Spatial questions require tracking invariants through transformations rather than guessing from familiarity.

sections.title: Language and comprehension
sections.body: For grammar, identify subject, verb, modifiers and required agreement. Distinguish possession (their), contraction (they’re) and location (there). For passages, separate explicit statements from reasonable but unsupported assumptions. An inference must follow from the passage, not merely be plausible in real life. Analogy questions should preserve the exact relationship, such as increasing intensity or part-to-whole.

sections.title: Analytical constraints
sections.body: Translate clues into explicit relations: before, immediately before, adjacent or not adjacent are different. Draw positions, place fixed clues, then enumerate remaining possibilities systematically. In circular seating, rotationally equivalent arrangements may be treated as the same, but reflection equivalence depends on the question. Use a counterexample arrangement to test whether a claim must always hold.

sections.title: Spatial transformations
sections.body: A rotation preserves orientation/chirality and pairwise distances; a reflection reverses handedness. For cube nets, track which faces become opposite, then rule out options placing opposite faces adjacent. When counting figures, classify by size and position so overlaps are included without counting the same figure twice. Explicit sketches are useful working tools.

examples.prompt: Three positions with A immediately before B and C after B

steps.title: Set up the state
steps.explanation: A,B must occupy adjacent positions in that order. The pair can start only at position 1 or 2 in a three-position arrangement.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: C must lie to their right, so A,B cannot occupy positions 2,3. If the pair occupies 2,3 there is no position right of B for C. This eliminates that case rather than merely making it unlikely.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.explanation: Only A,B,C remains. Replacing “immediately” with “somewhere” would weaken the adjacency requirement. The surviving arrangement satisfies both adjacency and the after-B condition.

examples.strategy: Translate “immediately before” into an adjacent ordered pair and apply the remaining position constraint.
examples.answer: Only A,B,C remains. Replacing “immediately” with “somewhere” would weaken the adjacency requirement.
examples.verification: In A,B,C, B follows A immediately and C is right of B. All three positions are filled exactly once.

steps: The noun books needs a possessive determiner.
Their means belonging to them; they’re expands to they are and cannot fill that noun-modifying role.
There describes location. Choose using grammatical function, not sound.

pitfalls: Do not add unstated constraints.
Immediately before differs from before.
A mirror image need not be obtainable by rotation.

checks.prompt: Three people A,B,C stand in a line. A must immediately precede B, and C must be after B. How many valid orders exist?
checks.hint: Try every location for the A,B pair.
checks.explanation: Only A,B,C satisfies both constraints.

checks.prompt: Four distinct people stand in a line without restrictions. How many arrangements are possible?
checks.hint: Use factorial ordering.

lessons.method:
Verbal questions can test grammatical structure, word meaning or comprehension. For grammar, identify subject/verb agreement, modifier attachment and parallel constructions before selecting a phrase that merely sounds familiar. Pronoun reference and tense should remain consistent with the intended sentence. Homophones such as their/there/they’re have different grammatical functions.
For comprehension, distinguish a passage’s explicit statement from an inference supported by it and from an outside fact that merely seems plausible. Words such as all, some, only and usually differ in logical strength. A conclusion stronger than its evidence may be invalid even when it matches real-world expectations.
Read each option against the exact passage and identify the supporting or contradicting phrase. A main-idea answer should cover the central argument rather than one memorable example. For word substitution, reread the complete sentence to ensure syntax and meaning both fit. GATE marks often turn on scope or qualification, so preserve uncertainty rather than strengthening a tentative claim into certainty. Analytical reasoning turns verbal conditions into restrictions on positions, groups or choices. Define the entities and allowed slots, then separate absolute constraints from relative ones. “Immediately before” imposes adjacency and order; “before” alone permits gaps. “Only if” expresses necessity and cannot be freely reversed.
Use a small table or case split for the most restrictive relationship. Propagate its consequences before assigning unrelated variables. Eliminate a case with one contradiction, but retain every still-feasible case when the question asks what could occur. A unique answer requires proving alternatives impossible, not just finding one feasible arrangement.
Track quantifiers in options: “must” holds in every feasible configuration, “can” in at least one and “cannot” in none. If information is insufficient, the correct result may be multiple configurations rather than an invented tie-break. For GATE, checking each proposed final arrangement against every original condition is a reliable final guard against an overlooked adjacency or exclusivity requirement. Spatial reasoning follows how locations and orientations change under transformations. A rotation moves every point around an axis/center by a common angle and preserves handedness; a reflection mirrors across an axis/plane and reverses handedness. An object that looks similar after moving is not necessarily obtainable by the allowed transformation.
For a square grid, label positions and map coordinates rather than trying to remember the image. A quarter-turn permutes corners and directions consistently; a mirror exchanges opposite sides relative to its axis. Apply transformations to every distinctive mark, then compare with the candidate. For cubes, opposite faces never become adjacent under rotation and shared edges remain shared.
Avoid using an unrestricted mirror to justify an option when only rotation is permitted. Repeating four quarter-turns returns a planar figure to its start, giving a useful check. In GATE, asymmetric markers can distinguish transformations that a plain square cannot. A precise coordinate table reduces mental-visualization errors and exposes whether an option preserves the structure required by the problem. example.prompt: Choose the word in “The students brought ___ books”: their, there or they’re.
example.strategy: Identify role → Expand candidate → Compare meanings

steps.title: Identify role
steps.explanation: The blank modifies the noun books and needs a possessive determiner.

steps.title: Expand candidate
steps.explanation: They’re means they are, which does not fit that noun-modifying slot.

steps.title: Compare meanings
steps.explanation: Their means belonging to them; there indicates location.

example.answer: Their.

example.prompt: A,B,C occupy three positions. A is immediately before B and C is after B.
example.strategy: Possible pair locations → Eliminate second pair → Remaining placement

steps.title: Possible pair locations
steps.explanation: A,B can occupy 1,2 or 2,3.

steps.title: Eliminate second pair
steps.explanation: If B is at 3, there is no position after it for C.

steps.title: Remaining placement
steps.explanation: A=1,B=2,C=3 satisfies both conditions.

example.answer: Only A,B,C is feasible.
example.verification: Replacing immediately before by before weakens a constraint; preserve the wording when generalizing the method.

example.prompt: Rotate the 2×2 labeled grid with top row A B and bottom row C D clockwise by 90°.
example.strategy: Corner mapping → Other corners → Read transformed rows

steps.title: Corner mapping
steps.explanation: Top-left A moves to top-right; top-right B moves to bottom-right.

steps.title: Other corners
steps.explanation: Bottom-left C moves to top-left; bottom-right D moves to bottom-left.

steps.title: Read transformed rows
steps.explanation: The new top row is C A and bottom row D B.

example.answer: Clockwise result: top C A; bottom D B.
example.verification: Repeating this mapping four times restores A B / C D; a vertical mirror would instead give B A / D C.
